en: Preface to the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra-fayi* (The Unveiling of the Heart of the Perfection of Wisdom Sutra).
As for the teaching of Prajñā, it is vast and expansive, filling the void and encompassing all things;

its manifold dharma-gates include all that can be explained, and its manifold causal practices include all that must be cultivated. It summarizes the myriad phenomena of the ten realms—both the environment and the beings therein—and gathers all forms...
The two characters for "mind" open up countless paths of skillful means and illuminate the single emptiness of the five aggregates.

They sweep away the many attachments of the human heart and dispel the confusion of the six realms. When what is called "object" and what is called "mind" are both fused without distinction, then whether ordinary or holy, all are equally one as such.
This is precisely what is meant by the statement that all phenomena, from the very beginning, are eternally characterized by quiescence; how could they possibly be otherwise?
How can words and letters reach this? In the past, when the World-Honored One ascended the seat and remained silent for a long while, Mañjuśrī addressed the assembly, saying:
"Observe closely the Dharma of the Dharma-King; the Dharma of the Dharma-King is thus. This is the ocean of the Tathāgata’s non-speaking, where the great assembly has nothing to hear;
this is truly the time for the preaching of Prajñā. Alas, how much more vexed must those of dull and shallow capacity be!

The Venerable One moved his lips and stirred his tongue, raising waves where there was no wind; observing the capacities of both the small and the great, he preached the teachings of the gradual and the sudden.
Thus, he expounded the distinctions of the five periods, all of which ultimately converge in the One Vehicle; he established the differences of the nine realms, yet all alike reach the Buddha-realm.
Now, as for this sutra, its text is most concise while its meaning is most vast; it is difficult to exhaust its profundity, and those who explain it merely touch its surface.
To explain its title: just as among the hundred parts of a human body, the four limbs and especially the heart are the most vital, it is called the *Heart Sūtra*.

Furthermore, since *prajñā* is the innate, enlightened mind possessed by sentient beings, which has been obscured by the five aggregates for many kalpas, this sūtra teaches the method of "contemplating and seeing" to reveal, instruct, awaken, and lead one to the realization of crossing to the other shore; thus it is called the *Heart Sūtra*. Now, as for this sūtra...
From antiquity down to the present day, commentaries have been produced in great numbers; some are diffuse and muddled, while others are like "drawing snakes and adding legs.

My own prolixity here largely relies on personal conjecture. Within this work, I have already divided the teachings of both persons and dharmas into four schools each to expound their meanings, titling it *Fayi* (Revealing the Hidden);
yet, upon what was already complete, I have added yet more legs. I venture to reveal but a single glimpse for inspection.
[The Master] smiled and chided him.
On the latter part of the fifth month of the eighth year of the Chongzhen era, the year being Yi Hai,
the bhikṣu Zhengxiang Tiri composed this "Unveiling the Obscurities" for the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*.
The Monk Zhengxiang, a later student of the Tiantai teachings, provides this commentary.

△ First, the explanation of the title of the sutra. Whenever the Great Master of the Shanjia school explains the title of a sutra, he first establishes the Fivefold Profound Meaning (*wǔzhòng xuányì*):
1. Explaining the Name; 2. Discerning the Essence; 3. Clarifying the Thesis; 4. Discussing the Function; 5. Judging the Doctrinal Characteristics. Now, as for...
To explain: when the Dharma is taught, it must have a name; a name must manifest its essence; the essence is manifested through the thesis (*siddhānta*);
and the thesis achieves utility through its application. These five stages are like obtaining the main rope of a net or the collar of a garment;

the purport of a single sutra thus becomes vividly clear before one's eyes. In this present sutra, "Single Dharma" is the name, "True Reality" (*bhūtatathatā*) is the essence, and "Mahayana Cause" is the thesis.
The fruit is the thesis (*siddhānta*), the crossing over suffering is the function, and the refined butter (*sarpis*) is the characteristic of the teaching.
First, regarding the explanation of the title, there are both general and specific [aspects]. Generally, the twelve divisions of the teachings are collectively termed "Sūtra.

Specifically, there are seven ways of establishing a title—whether by a single element, a combination of two, or the complete set of three. The present sūtra is titled by means of a single dharma. In the Sanskrit language...

*Prajñā*, translated into Chinese as "wisdom" (*zhìhuì*), is also called "pure wisdom" (*jìng huì*). "Wisdom" takes the meaning of "illumination and clear understanding," a quality common to both ordinary beings and sages.
"Pure wisdom" takes the meaning of "transcending the entanglements" (*chán*), as it directly illuminates the principle (*lǐ*).

Because this wisdom destroys all deluded thoughts and accords with the ultimate perfection of the principle, it is without division; yet, for the sake of differentiation, three types are distinguished. The first is *prajñā* of the true mark (*shíxiàng*).

First is the contemplation of the essence of principle; second is the contemplation of the illumination of prajñā, which is the wondrous wisdom capable of observing; third is the prajñā of words, which refers to the expressed meanings of both exoteric and esoteric phrases.

Though divided, they are not separate, being but a single body with three names for its functions. It is neither three nor one, yet as three and as one, these two meanings are perfectly manifest. Thus it is said: The essence of principle is the fundamental nature; The illumination of prajñā is the wondrous wisdom that observes;

The prajñā of words consists of the exoteric and esoteric phrases and meanings. Though divided, they are not separate, being but a single entity. There are three names for its functions, yet it is neither three nor one. As three and as one, these two meanings are clearly present.

It is not translated [by a specific term]. Furthermore, *prajñā* refers to the realization of the ultimate principle upon fruition; it is profoundly deep and differs from its light and thin state during the causal stage.
Because it is weighty, it is not translated [by a specific term]. As for *pāramitā*, the Chinese translation is "reaching the other shore" (*dào bī'àn*).

In contrast to this, "the other" (*bi*) refers to that shore. This *prajñā* is of one substance between sage and ordinary person, and shares the same root between self and others, pervading all with purity.
Purity is fundamentally without "this" or "that"; it is simply to illuminate with the pure mind without falling into quiescence.
When a single thought moves delusively, the notions of self and other arise, giving rise to afflictions (*kleśa*). Based on these afflictions, birth and death (*saṃsāra*) grow;
birth and death are established as this shore, afflictions as the middle current, and *nirvāṇa* as the further shore. Each of the four teachings and four gates discusses them accordingly.
Those who embrace long-lasting delusion without awakening, dwelling amidst manifold sufferings while accepting them as their own lot, are the ordinary beings on this shore.
Those who understand the three emptinesses and achieve liberation for themselves, cultivating the truths and conditions to attain realization, are the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

Although they have escaped the suffering of birth and death (the *pariccheda-skandha*), because they still dwell on this shore of the *pariṇāma-śarīra* (the body of transformation), they must sever the dust-like afflictions of the various realms through the illumination of wisdom.
Those Bodhisattvas who analytically discern the principle and partially realize the three virtues still dwell on the shore of the *pariṇāmika-śarīra* (the body of transformation);

even upon reaching the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), they are said to have "arrived but not yet reached the ultimate. This is discussed in relation to the three preceding teachings.
However, from the superior perspective of the Perfect Teaching (*yāna*), birth-and-death is itself nirvāṇa; since there is no extinction to be realized, there is thus no "arrival."
Upon arriving, one observes that both birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are equally like illusions and dreams; this is what is meant by "perfect bodhi returns to non-attainment.
The "mind" (citta) is the very substance being examined, and it has three distinctions: first, the physical heart-mass (*māṃsa-guḍa-citta*);
second, the mind of conceptualization and deliberation (*ālambana-citta*); and third, the numinous knowing mind (*prajñā-citta*). As for the physical heart-mass, it is [the result of] the father...
That which is born from the mother’s blood and qi and currently resides within the five viscera is merely the locus where the two minds are attached.
As for the *yuanlü* (discursive) mind, it is that which presently discriminates while confronting the objects of the six sense-fields.

As for the *lingzhì* (spiritual-intuitive) mind, it blends amidst a thousand differences without confusion; it spans ten thousand ages with enduring presence, vertically exhausting the three periods of time.
It neither comes nor goes, yet it extends horizontally throughout the ten voids without deficiency or excess;
it does not increase in the state of sages nor decrease in the realm of ordinary beings. That which is confused by the first two minds is termed "deluded consciousness";
that which does not mix these three minds is termed "awakening"; and that which fuses the two minds into a single essence is termed "realization. Ordinary beings recognize...
If even the "fleshly heart" is still deluded regarding its objects of perception, how much more so the "spiritual knowing" [of external paths]?

These heterodox outsiders take the mind of discursive perception for spiritual knowing, and they mistake the state of turbid agitation for the nature of the mind. Once deluded, they take this as their mind and are certain that it resides within the physical body;
yet they do not realize that from the external world out to empty space, mountains, rivers, and the great earth, all are the wondrous [mind].

To clarify what appears within the mind: sentient beings undergo the suffering of birth and death amidst profound, lucid, and numinous awareness, whereas the Tathāgata eternally dwells in nirvāṇa amidst the triviality of birth and death.
Therefore, the various Dharma gates that are expounded are all for the sake of this mind. "Sūtra" is the general name for an era’s teachings; it is a term from the Sanskrit language.

*Sūtra* is translated as "Kie-king" (Sagely Scripture), because it accords with principle and accords with the capacities of sentient beings. Furthermore, "King" (Sūtra) is glossed as "Dharma" and "Constant.
It is called "Dharma" because the ten realms follow the same track; it is called "Constant" because it does not change throughout the three periods of time.

Moreover, it is the sacred instruction proclaimed from the Golden Mouth [of the Buddha], and is thus termed a "Sūtra. Second, the analysis of the essence (*tattva*) refers to the principle elucidated by this particular sūtra.

The *Dīpaṃkara-sūtra* states: "The characteristic of the emptiness of all dharmas is that emptiness is non-existence; the characteristic of no-characteristic is called the true characteristic (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
This is the *bhūtalakṣaṇa-prajñā* among the three types of *prajñā*. Ultimately, the ultimate goal of the later schools culminates in this;
in terms of function, it is initiated from this source of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*). Because it is the primary seal of the correctness of all dharmas, it is the true characteristic.

This is the essence of the Sūtra. ○ Third, regarding the "Principle" (zong): the wisdom of contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā*) is the cause for reaching the goal, and ultimate *nirvāṇa* is the fruit to be reached.
The principle that "practice arises entirely from nature" is the principle within the category of essence;

the principle that "essence is entirely within practice" is the essence within the category of principle. Practice at its inception is the cause, and practice at its culmination is the fruit. Practice.

Since it begins with the illumination of the emptiness of the aggregates as the causal practice and culminates in ultimate *nirvāṇa* as the fruit, the Mahāyāna cause and effect constitute the central tenet of this sutra.
Fourth, regarding its function: through the *prajñā* of words, the principle is revealed by means of the text;
through the principle, practice is initiated; thereby one transcends the two deaths, crosses over the middle stream, and delivers all from suffering and calamity.
Ultimate *nirvāṇa* is attained through this sutra; thus, the power and function of this sutra lie in its ability to deliver one from suffering and calamity.

V. Regarding the classification of the teachings (*jiao-xiang*): "Teaching" refers to the words of the Sage directed toward those below; "classification" refers to the discernment of similarities and differences.
There are five distinct periods [of teaching]: the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Āgama*, the *Vaipulya*, and so forth. The *Avataṃsaka* encompasses the *Āgama*, while the *Vaipulya* stands in contrast to them.
The *Prajñāpāramitā*, the *Dharmapada*, the *Lotus Sūtra*, and the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* are pure and without admixture;
this present sūtra belongs to the fourth period, universally encompassing the three teachings of the Mahāyāna, yet its primary intent lies in the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*). Thus concludes the title.
△ Second, the explanation of the scriptural text, in three parts: first, the structural division. It is the regular practice for all sutras to divide the text into three sections:

the introduction (nidāna), the main body (dharmadeśanā), and the dissemination (parīndanā). In this present sutra, the text is concise while the meaning is vast; it lacks an introductory section at the beginning and lacks a section on dissemination at the end.
Now, wishing to provide an explanation, I shall propose dividing it into three segments, following roughly the example of the *Śāriputraparipṛcchā-sūtra* (The Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching).
Regarding the initial introductory section (*nidāna*) of this sutra: it lacks a general introduction (*sāmānyanidāna*) and possesses only a specific introduction (*viśeṣanidāna*).

Alternatively, it may be that the general introduction was omitted by the translators of the Great Collection (*Mahāsannipāta*). The specific introduction extends from the passage on Avalokiteśvara down to the phrase "deliverance from all suffering and calamity.
Furthermore, among the two commentaries by Xianshou and Gushan, one states that it briefly indicates the essential framework, while the other states that it is based upon...

The practice of establishing the intention is uniform throughout this [text]. Second, from "Śāriputra, form is not different from emptiness" up to "this is the mantra of the unequaled," which is the main body of the teaching;
the phrase "the mantra that can eliminate all suffering" constitutes the dissemination (*pravartana*). Regarding the location where this sutra was preached:

one tradition says it was spoken within the "profound secret treasury" (*gambhīra-rahasya-garbha*), such as in the *Perfect Enlightenment Sutra* (*Ārya-bodhicitta-uttaratantra-sūtra*); another tradition says...
Regarding the location of the royal city and Vulture Peak, according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, it should be at Vulture Mountain. △ Second, the translators:
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Tang Dynasty, by imperial decree.
He was the master who translated the scriptures of these seven Buddhas. Tradition holds that he was an emanation of the Buddha Candana, though this has not yet been fully verified.
The Great Master’s secular surname was Chen; he was a native of Yingchuan and a descendant of Zhonggong. He possessed innate knowledge and could not forget anything after a single reading.
In his youth, he studied the Confucian classics; in his prime, he investigated the Indian texts (*zhufun*). He searched through seventeen cycles of treatises.
After more than one hundred years had passed, in the nineteenth year of the Zhenguan era, the pine branch turned eastward.

The assembly of practitioners welcomed it back, and by imperial decree, it was brought to Hongfu Monastery for translation, as recorded in detail in the biographies. In total, there have been five translations:
first, that translated by Kumārajīva, titled the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Mahāvidyāmantra Sūtra*; second, this very one, translated by Master Xuanzang.
The translations of the titles by the three masters—Śīlendrabodhi, Prajñāvarman, and Ye-shes-sde—are identical to those of Master Xuanzang.
The title translated by Dharmachandra is *Sarvajñātākośa-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, and that translated by Śīlavarman is *Buddhabhāṣita-ārya-prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*.
The version now being commented upon follows the translation of Master Xuanzang for two reasons.
Therefore, what is it? Master Xuanzang, during his journey to and from India, took this scripture as a means to wash away obstacles.

Those who have transmitted and upheld it throughout the two worlds all rely upon this text; the details of his travels through those countries are fully recorded in his biography (*Xiyuji*), so they shall not be cited here at length.
△ Third, the actual explanation of the scriptural text. Part One: The Introduction. Sub-part One: Identifying the practitioner.
The person.
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
This is the preface by the scribe regarding those who are first able to practice this [path], including their causes and fruits, both general and specific, as they contemplate themselves.
"Abiding" (*zài*) refers to the cultivation of causes that result in sublime titles. The three wisdoms arise within a single mind, and the three truths are illuminated within a single mind.

Abiding in emptiness does not depart from the provisional and the middle; abiding in the provisional does not differ from emptiness and the middle; and abiding in the middle simultaneously illuminates both emptiness and the provisional.

These are perfectly interfused and unimpeded, for none are produced through deliberate mental effort (*manasikāra*); therefore, they are called "sovereign" (*svatantra*). This sovereignty is the true self (*ātman*), and this true self is non-existent.
"I" is that which is not "not-I," for this is the true aspect (*dharmatā*); thus it is said, "Self-Existent," which explains the cause. Furthermore, regarding "Avalokiteśvara":
"Avalokita" (Contemplation) is the wisdom of contemplation that issues forth from the essence of the true aspect as the wisdom of the Middle Way;

because this wisdom of the Middle Way illuminates the principle of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), it is called "Avalokita. "Īśvara" (Lord) refers to the object of contemplation, which is the ten realms.
Regarding the principle that his voice accords with the various sounds of beings, he manifests whatever body is necessary to deliver them and preaches the Dharma accordingly.
The thirty-four sacred forms appear simultaneously, neither before nor after, like the single moon in the sky whose reflection appears in ten thousand waters;
therefore, he is called Avalokiteśvara. This explains his title as a fruition. As for the general [meaning], it refers to ordinary...
Those who cultivate Prajñā maintain the constant truth in every thought-moment and bring the illusory dust of sensory objects to rest within every mind;
because the objective realm and contemplation are as one without deviation, they are said to possess "sovereign mastery.

As for the distinction, it is that Bodhisattvas have already cultivated and realized [this state], leaving behind a mirror of wisdom for the age of images, so that future generations may cultivate and realize it, providing a model and standard for the final dharma-age. △ Second.
Regarding the dharma to be practiced:
when practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the practitioner cultivates this;
cultivating this is the practice of *śamatha* for one's own benefit, while practicing this is the practice of *kuśala* for the sake of transforming others—this is what is shown.
This is the method for cultivation and realization. This Prajñā cannot be understood by those of shallow knowledge—neither ordinary worldlings nor even those of the Two Vehicles;
it is therefore called "profound. As for the term "time," it refers to the moment when the faculties [of the practitioner] and the principle [of the teaching] are in accord.

If explained according to the teachings (*yàojiào*), there are two types of Prajñā, distinguished as common and uncommon. Regarding this Prajñā, its relative shallowness and depth are discussed in succession.

The former is shallow and the latter is progressively deeper; the general meaning lies solely in the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), which penetrates to the very source of all phenomena through perfect cultivation, perfect severance, and perfect realization.
Thus it is said to be "deep. As the *Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment* states: "To know illusion is to be detached from it, requiring no expedient means;
to be detached from illusion is awakening itself, with no gradual stages. △ Third, showing the correct cultivation, part one: initial illumination and vision.
Second, the five aggregates; third, all are empty; fourth, transcending all suffering and calamity. First is "contemplating and seeing":
contemplating and seeing that the five aggregates are all empty, one transcends all suffering and calamity.
"Contemplating" (zhào) refers to the wisdom that is able to contemplate; "seeing" (jiàn) refers to the realm that is contemplated. One contemplates with the four wisdoms through a single path.
First, through the wisdom of insight (*prajñā-jñāna*), one perceives the true nature of the Path, shatters all phenomenal forms (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*), and opens up the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;

second, through the knowledge of the modes of all paths (*sarva-mārga-ākāra-jñatā*), one knows the distinct characteristics of delusion and awakening within the ten dharma-realms, sweeps away the phenomenal forms of the environment and inhabitants of the ten dharma-realms, and reveals the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
third, through the knowledge of all things (*sarvajñatā*), one knows that all dharmas are entirely quiescent and detached.

Because one awakens to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision through all moving signs; because one enters the Buddha’s knowledge and vision through the single-characteristic dharma known by the fourfold omniscience—a single characteristic that is quiescent, equal, non-dual, and free from the characteristics of differentiation; and because the preceding stages are coarse while the succeeding stages are subtle. As for the five aggregates (*skandha*), they consist of form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; these are the objects illuminated by wisdom. The aggregate of form is so called because it is a collection (*caya*) of various types of matter. The aggregate of sensation is so called because it is a collection of the three kinds of feeling. The aggregate of perception is so called because it is a collection of the grasping of marks. The aggregate of mental formations is so called because it is a collection of volitions. The aggregate of consciousness is so called because it is a collection of cognitions. These are the meanings of the term "aggregate. Furthermore, because they are the basis for the arising of suffering, they are called aggregates. Because they are the basis for the arising of the views of self and what belongs to self, they are called aggregates. Because they are the basis for the arising of the afflictions, they are called aggregates. Because they are the basis for the arising of karma, they are called aggregates. Because they are the basis for the arising of birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, they are called aggregates. Because they are the basis for the arising of all conditioned phenomena, they are called aggregates. Because they are the basis for the arising of all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*), they are called aggregates. Because they are the basis for the arising of all obstacles to the Three Non-attachments, they are called

"Accumulation" (*skandha*) is its meaning: because the nature of wisdom is empty and quiescent, it causes the accumulation of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) to become constricted and obstructed;
thus, "aggregate" (*skandha*) takes the sense of covering. Because *prajñā* is numinous and luminous, it causes the covering of the five aggregates to become deluded and darkened.

As for "form" (*rūpa*), it refers to the two types of retribution—the primary and the secondary—anything that can be grasped by the eye is called form. Receiving the influence and reflection of form as it enters the mind is called "feeling" (*vedanā*).

To contemplate each [object] one by one is called *saṃjñā* (perception); to give rise to attachment is called *saṃskāra* (volitional formations); to discriminate between the beautiful and the ugly is called *vijñāna* (consciousness).
The first aggregate (*skandha*) belongs to the body, while the remaining four belong to the mind. Viewing them together, they are comprised of the two terms "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*).

For those whose delusion regarding the mind is heavy, the Buddha opened the mind into four: feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness; for those whose delusion regarding form is heavy, he opened form into ten categories.
To expand "form" (*rūpa*) into six refers to the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*). When both form and mind are deluded, one expands them into the eighteen realms (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*).
Thus, the treatise says: "Within all the world, there are only name (*nāman*) and form; if one wishes to contemplate according to reality, one should contemplate only name and form.
"All are empty" means to clearly perceive (*pratyavekṣate*). The arising of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) is like water forming [ice].

When ice is illuminated by light, it is seen to be entirely empty; it is like hot water melting ice. Once the ice has melted, there is nothing else that can cause its disappearance—it is simply water.

Therefore, it is said that all is empty. As for "crossing over all suffering and calamity": all sentient beings are shrouded and obstructed by the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), which darken their nature of wisdom.
Taking a state of confusion and agitation as their own mind-nature, they crawl through the three realms and sink into them.
For two kalpas, one has endured various sufferings in the ocean of death, traveling all day long yet remaining unaware of it.
Now, observing that the five aggregates are empty, the internal permeation of *prajñā* awakens the fundamental luminosity; this brilliance stands out preeminent, utterly shattering [delusion].
Both birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are seen as mere illusions and dreams. It is neither an arrival nor a crossing over—what reality could there be in suffering and calamity? This...
The Sūtra author narrates the following section on the True Doctrine (saddharma) to correctly demonstrate the method for illuminating and seeing [reality].
△ Second, the Section on the True Doctrine (saddharma-bhāga), in eight parts: 1. Summoning the Appropriate Audience; 2. Correctly Demonstrating the Method and Rules;

3. General Examples; 4. The Five Aggregates (skandhas); 5. Directly Revealing the Emptiness of Nature; 6. Emptiness and the Non-existence of the Five Aggregates; 7. Opening up Form for those of dull faculties and showing them distinct illumination.
The seven seals, the eight, the four mantras, the citations, and the conclusion. First, the invocation of the appropriate recipient: Śāriputra.

"Śāri" means "Son of the Vulture" (Gṛdhraputra) in Chinese; that is, it is the name in the Tang language. This is an instance where both the Chinese and Sanskrit terms are presented together; he is the person being addressed.
One tradition says that Śāriputra was named after his mother’s physical form; another says he was named after his mother’s beautiful eyes.
This sutra primarily transforms bodhisattvas while incidentally including those of the two vehicles. Now, Śāriputra is the foremost in wisdom among the assembly;
calling him forth and addressing him specifically reveals that this profound *prajñā* cannot be bestowed upon anyone lacking such wisdom, let alone upon ordinary beings of inferior capacity.

...Thus it is. △ Second, the actual presentation of the methodological rules, in four parts: first, following the text; second, in terms of persons; third, in terms of teachings; fourth, the explanation via the three contemplations.
Form is not different from emptiness, and emptiness is not different from form; form is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself form.

This is the passage concerning "the clear observation that the five aggregates are all empty. Regarding phenomena (*dharma*), there are four categories; regarding persons (*pudgala*), there are four types of faculties—sharp or dull;
wisdom has its levels of depth; and hindrances have their degrees of thickness. Where one's power does not reach, the stages are naturally differentiated.

As for "form" (*rūpa*), it refers to the illusory form of both the environment and the sentient beings; as for "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*), it is the emptiness of the nature of *prajñā*. Form is the characteristic of emptiness.
"Emptiness" means that the nature of characteristics arises from their substance; because characteristics and substance are fused, when one contemplates them, they are all empty.
△ Second, [the classification] according to persons has three parts: first, ordinary beings; second, those of the two vehicles; third, bodhisattvas.
"Form is not different from emptiness" means that one clearly perceives that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of ordinary beings are all empty.
As for the Dharma-medicine of the Tathāgata, it accords with the illnesses of sentient beings' attachments: to those who are deluded by form, emptiness is shown;

to those who become attached to the taste of emptiness, form is used in turn to break through that attachment. Thus, the dust of the passions is utterly swept away and attachment to phenomena is forgotten together; herein lies the true mind of *prajñā*.
It is revealed in its solitude. Since ordinary beings have possessed the consciousness-spirit, they have clung to illusory form as a real substance;
thus, they are not only deluded regarding true emptiness, but they do not even recognize illusory form. Why is this?

Because they cling to the illusory as real, it is shown to them that "form is not different from emptiness," so that by contemplating the non-difference of form and emptiness, they may accord with the Dharma and their deluded sentiments will naturally be dispelled.
This transcends the suffering and calamities of the limited birth-and-death within the shared realm.

That "emptiness is not different from form" means clearly perceiving that the five aggregates of the two vehicles are all empty. Yet, one must not be attached to form, nor should one be attached to emptiness.
By taking form as the substance of emptiness and clarifying emptiness through form, there is no form to be discarded; if one loathes form and seeks emptiness, one dwells in [a biased state].
However, those who cling to these as two distinct pillars do not realize that nature is inherently endowed with all phenomena. Therefore,

it is shown that "emptiness is not different from form," so that by contemplating how emptiness and form are non-different within the conditions of the Truths, attachment to dharmas is dissolved and forgotten, one accords with the Dharma,
and crosses over the sufferings and calamities of birth-and-death in the *parinirmita-vaśavartin* realm.
"Form is itself emptiness; emptiness is itself form" means that the Bodhisattva clearly perceives that the five aggregates are all empty.
While it was previously stated that they are "not different from emptiness," the present statement that they are "identical to emptiness" signifies a further advancement toward ultimate truth.

This identity of form and emptiness differs from the perspective of ordinary beings, and its radiant fundamental wisdom that shatters the mass of delusions differs from that of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. If it were not for the threefold contemplation (*trīṇi-vipaśyanā*), this would not be possible.
Through perfect interfusion, how can the coarse be immediately made sublime? It is shown that "form is emptiness" means the objective realm is identical to the mind;
"emptiness is form" means the mind is identical to the objective realm. Form and emptiness mutually interpenetrate, and both mind and object are empty.

When both person and phenomena are forgotten, affairs are exhausted and principle is perfected, thereby transcending the suffering and calamities of birth-and-death within the *parinirmita-vaśavartin* (real-retribution) land.
Third, regarding the classification by teaching (*yàojiào*): "Form is not different from emptiness" refers to the *zàng* (Āgama) teaching, which analyzes form to clarify emptiness;

this is for those of dull faculties among the Śrāvakas of the Small Vehicle. "Emptiness is not different from form" refers to the *tōng* (Shared) teaching, which takes form as its substance to enter into emptiness.

"Form is itself emptiness" refers to the *bié* (Distinct) teaching, which enters into the middle [reality] through successive stages. "Emptiness is itself form" refers to the *yuán* (Perfect) teaching, which simultaneously illuminates both the true and the conventional.
To enter the Middle Way from the mundane:
first, "form is not different from emptiness" means entering emptiness from the conventional; second, "emptiness is not different from form" means emerging from emptiness into the conventional;
the latter two, being mutually identical, constitute the perfect and wondrous Middle Way. This is the objective realm of the Mahāyāna gate in this present sutra.
Wisdom transcends dependence; from beginning to end, it is neither two nor three. Contemplating the one mind, it is said that there is a sequence;

yet when confronting objects, the cultivation of contemplation is the triad of three-in-one, perfectly interfused. This overcomes the Hinayana and the biased Bodhisattvas, causing their minds to become open and at ease, so that they may enter the subsequent *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
△ Third, the general analogy of the four aggregates.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
These four aggregates belong to the mind and arise in succession based on the preceding aggregate of form; there are sixteen such phrases in total.
The present text states "are also like this" as a summary thereof. △ Fourth, directly revealing the emptiness of nature.
"Śāriputra, all dharmas have the characteristic of emptiness: they are neither born nor extinguished, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing.

The preceding passage concluded with the contemplation of the five aggregates; now, to demonstrate that these are entirely empty, the text reiterates the address to the primary recipient, stating "all dharmas have the characteristic of emptiness," which refers to the true reality (*dharmatā*) of ultimate emptiness. "All dharmas" refers to the ten realms of existence (*daśadhātu*), including both the environments and...

This is the Dharma of the True Reality (*dharmatā*). The characteristic of emptiness is precisely the absence of characteristics; it lacks such characteristics as arising and ceasing, defilement and purity, increase and decrease.
Because its essence is eternally abiding, it has no arising or ceasing; because its essence is empty and harmonious, it has no defilement or purity;

because its essence is all-pervasive and perfect, it has no increase or decrease. Furthermore, the aforementioned five aggregates and so forth are the characteristics of *prajñā*, which is what is meant by "the greenness of green."
The verdant bamboos are all *tathatā*, and the lush yellow flowers are none other than *prajñā*. It is further said:

"All dharmas, from their very origin, are eternally characterized by quiescent extinction. Thus, through non-difference they appear as different, and while the various dharmas appear different, they are not different;
the characteristics of the world are eternal. △ Fifth, revealing that there are no aggregates within emptiness.
Therefore, within emptiness there is no form, no sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;

that is to say, emptiness is the absence of the five aggregates. Since illusory appearances are empty, their true nature manifests spontaneously. A single color and a single fragrance are none other than the Middle Way;
a single movement and a single stillness directly reveal the fundamental reality. △ Six: Opening [the teaching] on Form for those of dull faculties.
Separately illuminating the first of the nine, the six sense faculties—namely, the absence of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—one perceives that these six faculties are all empty.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Originally, based on a single luminous intelligence, it is divided into six."
In this state of harmony, one now contemplates according to the essence itself; through the nature, cultivation is perfected, and the roots of causes manifest the nature.
Just as ice is water, there is nothing that is not *prajñā*; therefore, there are no six sense organs. △ Second, the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*).
There are no forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects;

he clearly perceives that the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) are all empty. When the sense-faculties (*indriya*) and sense-objects (*viṣaya*) mutually interpenetrate, they constitute the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), also known as the twelve entrances (*dvādaśāyatana*).

Ten of these bases belong to the category of form (*rūpa*), namely the five faculties, the five objects, and half of the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*); one base [the remaining half] belongs to the category of consciousness.
"Half belongs to the mind," meaning the entire sphere of the mental faculty (*manāyatana*) and one portion of the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).

These objects originally arise from the turbidification of the clear, tranquil ocean, triggered by the attachment to stillness that gives rise to vision and so forth. Now, by contemplating in accordance with their true nature, they are seen as nothing other than the single *prajñā*;
therefore, the six sense-objects do not exist. △ Third, the six consciousnesses.
There is no眼界 (eye-element) up to and including no意識界 (consciousness-element).
He clearly perceives that the eighteen elements (*dhātus*) are all empty. "Element" (*dhātu*) carries the meaning of "lineage" (*gotra*) as well as the meaning of "distinction.

These eighteen are opened for those who are deluded regarding both form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*). Fundamentally, there is but one consciousness; it becomes differentiated according to the sense-faculties (*indriya*). [The first] refers to the faculties and their objects (*viṣaya*).

Since consciousness (*vijñāna*) is also empty and thus becomes wisdom (*jñāna*), the six consciousnesses do not exist. These three categories [of aggregates, bases, and elements] illuminate and reveal that the five aggregates (*skandha*) of ordinary beings are all empty;
this follows the preceding phrase, "form is not different from emptiness. △ Forty-two: Dependent Origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
There is no ignorance, nor is there the exhaustion of ignorance; and so on, up to there being no old age and death, nor the exhaustion of old age and death.

He clearly perceived that the twelve links of dependent origination are all empty. "Dependent origination" means that they successively induce results as causes and mutually rely upon one another as conditions, beginning from the absence of ignorance up to the absence of old age and death—this is the arising of the twelve links of dependent origination.
The marks of the exhaustion of ignorance up to the exhaustion of old age and death constitute the cessation of the twelve links of dependent origination.
Having realized that these phenomena of arising and ceasing are, in their very essence, neither produced nor extinguished, they are said to be "non-existent. △ 5. The Four Noble Truths.
There is no suffering, its origin, its cessation, or the path.

One clearly perceives that the Four Noble Truths are all empty. Suffering refers to the shifting of the three characteristics: birth, change, and extinction. Its origin refers to the movement of the four mental states:
greed, hatred, delusion, and the equanimous state. Cessation refers to the extinction of existence and its return to non-existence. The path refers to the antidote.

Curing that which is easily usurped refers to suffering and its accumulation (*duḥkha-samudaya*), which are the causes and effects of the mundane; the path and cessation (*mārga-nirodha*) are the causes and effects of the supramundane.

These constitute the four truths of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-vyaya-catur-āryasatya*) according to the *Hīnayāna* teachings. Furthermore, there are the [truths of] non-arising and the immeasurable;

here, we shall address the four truths of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra-catur-āryasatya*) according to the Perfect Teaching (*Vimalakīrti*). Karmic fetters are themselves liberation, so there is no suffering to be loathed; worldly toil is fundamentally pure, so there is no accumulation to be [abandoned].
The severing of afflictions is itself bodhi; there is no path to be cultivated. Birth and death are themselves nirvana; there is no extinction to be realized.

Therefore, it is said that they "do not exist. This refers to the insight that the truths and conditions of the two vehicles are all empty, which corresponds to the preceding statement that "emptiness is not different from form. △ Six: The Six Paramitas.
There is neither ignorance nor attainment;

one clearly perceives that the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) are all empty. Since wisdom (*prajñā*) constitutes the essence of the six perfections, when the perfection of wisdom is empty, the other five perfections are also empty;
hence it is said "neither. Furthermore, the wise person contemplates this wisdom, wherein the three types of wisdom are perfectly interfused as the omniscient wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*).
"Attainment" refers to the fact that the essential substance of the principle of the Three Truths is all-pervasive, such that both subject and object are simultaneously extinguished;
this is what is meant by the phrase "form is identical to emptiness, and emptiness is identical to form" cited above. △ Seventh, concluding the preceding and introducing the subsequent.
"Because there is nothing to be attained.
The three characters "because there is nothing to be attained" conclude the previous character "because" and initiate the subsequent text.
While the preceding text spoke of emptiness, or non-existence, or non-attainment, it now concludes with "nothing to be attained. △ Eight: Cultivation and Realization.
Regarding the persons and the dharma: "A Bodhisattva, by virtue of relying on the Prajñāpāramitā...
[In this context], "Bodhisattva" is the full Sanskrit designation; the term currently used, "Pusa," is an abbreviation formed by omitting the two characters *ti* and *tuō*.

In the language of China, this is called the Great Way that brings sentient beings to fulfillment; it is the self-realization of *prajñā* (wisdom) and its subsequent teaching to others, which is why it is present here.
This is the person capable of cultivation, and *prajñā* and the like are the dharmas upon which they rely. Among the three teachings, the Bodhisattva stands preeminent;
while their skillfulness or clumsiness differs, we shall now manifest [this] according to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). 9. The Fruit of the Perfection of Removing Obstacles.
When the mind is without hindrance, because there is no hindrance, there is no fear; one is far removed from inverted dreams and delusions, reaching ultimate nirvana.
This is the crossing over of all suffering and calamity. If one takes a mind that grasps at existence as the basis for cultivating the cause, it is like boring...

Torn rags moving among thorns encounter obstacles at every turn; yet, by illuminating the principle of perfect interfusion with a mind of non-attainment, one moves like a clear breeze through the great void—transverse and longitudinal, free and unimpeded. Thus, one achieves the virtue of liberation;
being without fear, one achieves the virtue of the Dharma-body; and being free from inverted dreams and delusions, one achieves the virtue of Prajñā-wisdom.
The three paths are not separate from yet are separated from [the three poisons], and the three virtues are not realized yet are realized;
only when there is non-attachment to each one does one depart from inversion, which is why it is called "ultimate nirvana. △ Seven: Certification.
The Buddhas of the three periods of time, by relying on the Prajñāpāramitā, have attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This reveals that it is not merely one Buddha, two Buddhas, three, four, or five Buddhas who have cultivated and realized this Prajñā; rather, [it has been so for ten...]
Throughout the three periods of time, there are no Buddhas who do not rely upon this to cultivate and realize it.

In the Sanskrit language, *anuttara* means "unsurpassed," and *samyak-saṃbodhi* means "right, equal, and perfect enlightenment. Because its merit and wisdom are perfectly complete, it is called "unsurpassed.
Because it distinguishes itself from the partial and small [vehicles] yet does not depart from them, it is called "right, equal, and perfect. It illuminates the three truths simultaneously.
Therefore, it is called "Perfect Enlightenment. △ Eighth: The Mantra is cited and concluded.
Thus one knows that the Prajñāpāramitā is a great divine mantra, a great illuminating mantra, an unsurpassed mantra, and an unequaled mantra.
This is the actual efficacy of the aforementioned "all five aggregates are empty. Ordinary beings are bound by the five aggregates like silkworms in their cocoons;

they cannot attain their true spirit. Now, through the illumination of Prajñā, one perceives that form is not different from emptiness and the mind is without hindrance—like a bird escaping its cage, it may be called "spiritual.
Therefore, it is said to be a "Great Divine Mantra" that attains the benefit of destroying evil.

This is the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint of therapeutic remedy). The "Great Bright Mantra" is the realization of the actual efficacy of the two vehicles' [realization] that the five aggregates are empty.

Although the practitioners of the two vehicles have destroyed the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and suppressed the *rajas-kaṣāya* (dust-like afflictions), having emerged from the three realms, because their ignorance (*avidyā*) remains entirely intact, they remain as if in a long night.
Now, it is said that Prajñā illuminates and perceives that emptiness is not different from form; thus, ignorance will... [be dispelled].
The nature of Nirvana has been shattered, and the sky shows a slight dawn; it may be called "luminous.
Thus it is said that this is the "Great Luminous Mantra," which brings the benefit of joy according to the *loka-saṃvṛti* (worldly) perspective.

That it is the "Unsurpassed Mantra" concludes the actual efficacy of both the general and specific teachings regarding the emptiness of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) for Bodhisattvas. It is the realization that the form cultivated by Bodhisattvas is itself emptiness.

Because these [three virtues] are superior to what precedes them, they are called "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*); yet compared to the perfect [enlightenment], they are inferior, and it is by this contrast that the excellence of the three virtues is revealed.

Their capacity to produce wholesome benefits for sentient beings constitutes the *puruṣa-śāsana* (the teaching for persons). As for the "Incomparable Mantra," it is the actual efficacy of the realization that the six perfections are all empty.
Although the ignorance of the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) is not yet exhausted—like the moon on the fourteenth day—the Bodhisattva enters into *nirvāṇa*.
Realization has not yet reached its ultimate perfection; now, by invoking Prajñā, ignorance is suddenly emptied and the three virtues (triguṇa) are fully manifested.

Because nothing in the mundane or supramundane realms can equal it, it is called "unequaled" (asama); yet because it can transcend the unequal and accord with the myriad things, it is called the "equal-to-the-unequal" (asamasama) mantra.
To obtain entry into this principle is the benefit of the Paramārtha-siddhānta. △ Third, citing the universal exhortation.
The circulation [of this text] has two parts; first, the presentation of its function:
because it can eliminate all suffering and is truly not false, it is called the *prajñāpāramitā* mantra.
The wisdom of the Middle Way contemplation illuminates and shatters the three delusions, thereby accomplishing the three virtues (*triguṇa*) and eliminating the suffering of the nine dharma-realms.
He settles this by means of truthful speech; because the Tathāgata possesses five modes of expression—mentioning three and concealing two—it is called "truly real and not false.
This precisely means that even if the sun were made cold and the moon made warm, there would be no difference in what the Tathāgata has spoken.
He desires to cause sentient beings to enter into reality through sincere faith and to practice accordingly, so as not to allow them to harbor doubts. Furthermore...

Fearing that in this evil age the Māras would be powerful while the Dharma would be weak, he recited mantras to protect it, so that the four aforementioned actual effects and wisdoms would not be diminished;
for this reason, he spoke the mantras. △ Second, the recitation of the mantras.
He then spoke the mantra: *gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā*.
Among the five types of non-translation, this is the "secret" non-translation. Furthermore, "mantra" (*dhāraṇī*) means "to bless"; it is the Tathāgata’s blessing and aspiration.
I desire that all sentient beings may each attain realization and cultivate the path perfectly so that no one errs.

Furthermore, as for mantras, they are like secret passwords within an army; when the passwords correspond, there is no questioning or interrogation, but those who do not correspond are seized, rebuked, and executed. The Dharma of Prajñā is also like this: those who correspond are all Bodhisattvas.
That which is "incompatible" refers to Māra and externalists; furthermore, while the former is an explicit teaching of Prajñā, this is a secret teaching of Prajñā.

Regarding these two modes—explicit and secret—there are differences in the capacities of those to be trained; thus, what is appropriate for the explicit is taught explicitly, and what is appropriate for the secret is taught secretly.
In either case, it is solely for the purpose of enabling others to obtain benefit. For instance, within the explicit teachings, one obtains...

Those who benefit [others] exclusively by clinging to words, language, names, and signs—failing to eliminate conceptual thought and failing to sever their dwelling within the field of right and wrong—will never reach the end of their journey.
This is called the state of non-correspondence. Herein one hears the secret teaching:
it is that which has no place for attachment, which is free from the marks of names and free from the marks of speech, where the path of language is cut off and all deliberation is stilled.
This accords with the intent of Prajñāpāramitā—that there is neither speaking nor hearing—yet it is a profound teaching from which those who encounter it gain great benefit.

It is like the Zen school’s practice of single-mindedly investigating a single phrase that is devoid of meaning; it is like a wall of silver and a rampart of iron, causing one to suddenly sever the path of the mind.
It is like a thorn-bush of chestnuts, making one unable to swallow it; it is like a vajra-ring, making one... [unable to pass through].

If you cannot penetrate it, simply investigate in this manner until, through the exhaustion of knowledge and the cessation of doubt, there is a sudden realization like the bottom of a bucket falling away.
This is what is called "pushing open the door and falling through the lattice" without relying on external effort.

Reaching this point, where one joins in the beating of gongs and drums to manifest the True Constant, and strikes at doors and gates to return together to Prajñā, one may then follow conditions with ease and expansiveness.

Only when the mind is at ease and dwells together with the previously explained "head-entering" in its respective paths can one clearly perceive that the five aggregates are all empty and transcend all suffering and calamity.
*The Heart Sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom: Unveiling the Hidden* (End).
